Hugh Martin
HYOO MAR-tin
proper noun
Germanic given name Hugh, from hug, “heart, mind, spirit”; with the surname Martin, from the Latin Martinus, related to Mars, the god of war.

📖 Biblical Definition

Hugh Martin (1822–1885) was a Free Church of Scotland minister and theologian, trained in mathematics before he was given to the ministry, whose keen and ordered mind was consecrated to the deep things of the gospel. Compelled by ill health to lay down his pastoral charge, he gave his later years to writing, and in The Atonement—in its relations to the covenant, the priesthood, and the intercession of our Lord—he set forth with rare vigour the federal, substitutionary work of Christ, showing how the cross flows out of the eternal covenant of grace and is bound up with Christ’s priestly office and His unceasing intercession for those He redeemed. He would not let the atonement stand as a bare transaction but wove it into the whole counsel of God, that the shed blood and the pleading Advocate are one work for one people. His treatise on Jonah, reading that prophet as a type of Christ, breathes the same reverent, Christ-centred exposition. His labour teaches that the death of Christ is a definite, covenant redemption, that the Priest who died yet lives to intercede, and that the surest comfort of the believer is to know his sins were laid on a Substitute appointed in the everlasting covenant, whose finished sacrifice and living intercession together secure the salvation of all for whom He died.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Free Church theologian, author of The Atonement in its covenant and priestly relations.

expand to see more

Hugh Martin, 1822–1885, Free Church of Scotland minister and theologian, trained in mathematics.

Laid down his pastoral charge through ill health and gave his later years to writing.

Author of The Atonement, treating it in relation to the covenant, priesthood, and intercession of Christ.

A defender of the federal, substitutionary, definite redemption purchased by Christ.

Also wrote a Christ-centred exposition of the prophet Jonah as a type of the Redeemer.

📖 Key Scripture

Heb 7:25 — "Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them."

Joh 10:15 — "As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep."

Rom 8:34 — "Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us."

Heb 9:12 — "Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the covenant, priestly, definite atonement of Christ.

expand to see more

This entry is preserved because Martin’s labour rebukes every scheme that would sever the cross from the covenant and the priesthood, whether by making the atonement a general and indefinite thing or by dividing Christ’s dying from His living intercession.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the federal, substitutionary, and definite atonement of Christ—flowing from the everlasting covenant, wrought by His priestly sacrifice, and secured by His unceasing intercession—which is the sure ground of the believer’s comfort.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name joins the spirit-name Hugh to a martial Latin surname.

expand to see more

Hugh — from Germanic hug, “heart, mind, spirit.”

Martin — from Latin Martinus, related to Mars, the god of war.

The bearer lived 1822–1885, a Free Church theologian trained first in mathematics.

His treatise on the atonement made the surname a mark of covenant orthodoxy.

The name thus binds a consecrated mind to a warfare for the truth of the cross.

Usage

"Read Hugh Martin’s The Atonement to see the cross bound to covenant and priesthood."

"Cite Martin to defend the definite, substitutionary redemption of Christ for His sheep."

"Point to his treatise on Jonah as a model of typological, Christ-centred exposition."
